clue.text: Drink drop of sherry immediately before dance

indicators.note: a drop is only a tiny amount, so just the opening letter of the following word is used

blocks.note: the first letter of sherry
now means at once
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone at a party has a little sherry just before taking to the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just sets the order of the pieces. A snowball is a party cocktail of advocaat and lemonade, popular in Britain at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowball is a mixed cocktail, so it is a kind of drink.

clue.text: One involved in covering Garmisch's foremost sport

indicators.note: something involved in another is wrapped up inside it, so one item sits within the other
foremost means at the very front, so only the opening letter of the town name is used

blocks.note: skin is a body's outer covering
the Roman numeral for one
the first letter of Garmisch

explanation.surface: A sport that the Bavarian ski resort of Garmisch is famous for.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside SKIN to make SKIIN, then G is added. Garmisch-Partenkirchen is a German winter-sports resort, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiing is a winter sport practised on snow slopes.

clue.text: Soft toy did strange thing

indicators.note: soft material has no fixed shape and can be squashed into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cuddly soft toy did something weird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft toy' reads as one phrase, a teddy bear; 'Soft' is actually the signal to rearrange the letters of 'toy did'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddity is something peculiar or unusual, a curiosity.

clue.text: Withdraw support quietly — deal's off

indicators.note: something off has gone bad or wrong, so these letters are disordered

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
p is piano, the musical direction for quietly
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A backer quietly pulls their support because the deal has collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdraw support' looks like one phrase, but the definition is 'Withdraw' alone and 'support' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To backpedal is to retreat from a position or promise previously held.

clue.text: After lucky escapes, the eleven players perhaps give vent to anger

indicators.note: after places one piece behind another, so the second thing named comes first here

blocks.note: a let-off is a lucky escape from punishment
a cricket or football side has eleven players

explanation.surface: A team that kept getting away with things blows its top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' fixes the order: the second thing named is written first. 'Perhaps' marks eleven players as just one example, since a cricket or football side has eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: To let off steam is an idiom for releasing pent-up anger or energy, like a boiler venting pressure.

clue.text: Vital to reform a country

indicators.note: to reform something is to form it anew, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: It is essential that a nation undergoes reform.
explanation.definitionFit: Latvia is a Baltic nation in northern Europe.

clue.text: Player's agent blowing top

indicators.note: blowing its top means the word loses its head, so the first letter is lost

blocks.note: a factor is an agent who acts for another, especially in business

explanation.surface: A performer's agent loses their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowing top' suggests losing one's temper; here it removes the first letter of FACTOR. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is an old word for an actor, as in a troupe of players.

clue.text: Old carriage in London station

blocks.note: first meaning: a light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage
second meaning: a major railway terminus in central London

explanation.surface: A vintage carriage displayed in a London railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from Queen Victoria, after whom the carriage and the station were named.
explanation.definitionFit: A victoria was a horse-drawn carriage, and London Victoria is a mainline railway terminus.

clue.text: One deserting a position at end of battle

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
a post is a job or position
taken as written
the last letter of battle

explanation.surface: A soldier abandons their post as the fighting ends.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a military deserter, but the desertion is of a faith or cause.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostate is someone who abandons their religion or principles, a deserter of belief.

clue.text: Point out charge that involves a piece of espionage

indicators.note: to involve is to include or take in, so one item sits within the other
just one piece of the word is used, its opening letter

blocks.note: to indict is to charge formally with a crime
taken as written
the first letter of espionage

explanation.surface: A spy charge is laid out in detail.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside INDICT to make INDICAT; the E from espionage is then added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To indicate is to show or point to something.

clue.text: Reportedly unable to move old plaster

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said by others, so the sound is what counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: stuck means fixed in place
O is a standard abbreviation for old
the two pieces run together and spoken sound like the plaster's name

explanation.surface: Old plaster said to be firmly stuck in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' seems to describe the plaster but is a piece of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine plaster used to coat walls and make mouldings.

clue.text: Don gets upset with tennis call

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, turned the other way, so the phrase is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to don clothes is to put them on

explanation.surface: An Oxford don is irritated by an umpire's call at tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a university teacher but is the verb meaning put on.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, 'not up' is called when the ball has bounced twice before being returned.

clue.text: Understand dignitary's not in

blocks.note: a figure is a notable person, as in a public figure
out is the opposite of in

explanation.surface: Grasp that the important person is not at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To figure out is an idiom for working something out, grasping it.

clue.text: Stab awfully violent chap (not half!) in horror story

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so the letters are put into bad order
not half means only half of the word survives, the other half removed

blocks.note: a stab at something is a go, an attempt
taken as written, then rearranged
the first half of chap

explanation.surface: A man stabs someone savagely in a horror tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stab' looks like a violent verb but means an attempt. 'Not half!' is also British slang for 'very much so'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gothic novel is a genre of fiction with horror, gloom and the supernatural, like Frankenstein.

clue.text: Spread scandal — he did this maliciously, right?

indicators.note: doing something maliciously twists it in a harmful way, so the letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
Rt is an abbreviation of right

explanation.surface: Someone spreading gossip asks if a man acted spitefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay also loosely echoes the definition: a gossip claiming someone did something maliciously.
explanation.definitionFit: To dish the dirt is an idiom for passing on scandalous gossip.

clue.text: Extremely thin, came up with a diet that's different

indicators.note: something different is in another form, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone became skeletal after inventing an unusual diet.
explanation.definitionFit: Emaciated describes a body made abnormally thin, typically by starvation or illness.

clue.text: Usher brings confused lord back

indicators.note: confused means mixed up, so these letters are jumbled together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An usher shows a bewildered peer back to his seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a direction to reverse, but it is part of the letters to be mixed. Black Rod is the official who summons MPs to the House of Lords at the State Opening of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Black Rod is formally the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, a parliamentary officer.

clue.text: A US lawyer, male, drinking salt water

indicators.note: someone drinking takes liquid inside, so one item swallows the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a DA is a district attorney in the US
taken as written
S, as in the symbol for salt in the setter's shorthand

explanation.surface: An American attorney gulps seawater.
explanation.walkthrough: MALE takes S inside to give MSALE. 'Salt water' looks like one phrase, but only 'water' is the definition; taking S for salt is a loose abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam's ale is a jocular name for plain drinking water, the only drink the first man had.

clue.text: Dangerously ill, advocate in film

indicators.note: dangerously suggests something unstable and out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawyer in a film is seriously sick.
explanation.definitionFit: La Dolce Vita is Federico Fellini's 1960 Italian film about Rome's high life.

clue.text: Piece from Williamson, a tarantella

indicators.note: from means taken out of, so the letters are lifted straight out of the words that follow

blocks.note: the tail of Williamson, then a, then the start of tarantella

explanation.surface: A musical work by the composer Malcolm Williamson, a tarantella.
explanation.walkthrough: A tarantella is a fast Italian dance, so the musical surface is consistent.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a musical composition, and a piece is a general word for such a work.

clue.text: Ignore detour

blocks.note: first meaning: to go round or sidestep, as a verb
second meaning: a road taking traffic around a town, as a noun

explanation.walkthrough: The parts of speech differ: the first meaning is the verb, the second the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To bypass something is to avoid dealing with it, and a bypass is also a road routing traffic around an obstacle.

clue.text: Member of film crew arrived, then managed to screen The Graduate?

indicators.note: to screen is to shield or hide, so one piece is enclosed and concealed by another

blocks.note: came is the past tense of come, so arrived
to run a business is to manage it
an MA is a Master of Arts, held by a graduate

explanation.surface: A film crew turns up and shows The Graduate, the 1967 film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Graduate' looks like the 1967 film title but means a degree holder; the question mark flags that the degree is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameraman operates the camera, a key job on a film crew.

clue.text: Be king then abdicate, not having son

indicators.note: not having means doing without, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: to abdicate is to resign a throne
s is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A monarch rules for a while, then gives up the crown, leaving no heir.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes Edward VIII, who reigned then abdicated. RESIGN loses its S.
explanation.definitionFit: To reign is to rule as a monarch.

clue.text: Film director's trailer about Oregon

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: ivy is a trailing climbing plant
OR is the postal abbreviation for Oregon

explanation.surface: A director's film trailer concerns the state of Oregon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trailer' looks like a film preview but is a plant that trails. James Ivory directed A Room with a View.
explanation.definitionFit: James Ivory is an American film director, of the Merchant Ivory partnership.

clue.text: Member of rock band's crew in bar, one describing article on Ecstasy

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so these pieces encircle another
on means placed against or next to, so one piece is put right after the others

blocks.note: a rod is a bar of metal or wood
the Roman numeral for one
a is the indefinite article
E is slang for the drug Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A rock band's crew member, in a bar, describes a magazine piece about drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: RODI goes around A to give ROADI, and E is added. 'Article' looks like a magazine piece but is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadie sets up and transports equipment for a touring band.

clue.text: Russian girl with naval set at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Russian woman with a navy crowd out on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the naval scene, which hides its role as the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Svetlana is a common Russian woman's name.

clue.text: Expected girl to come back for governess

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way you came, so the name is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: due means expected, as in a train due at noon
Ann is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl is expected home, waiting for her governess.
explanation.definitionFit: A duenna is an older woman acting as chaperone or governess to girls, especially in Spain.

clue.text: Happy to attend fund-raisers in best clothes?

blocks.note: glad means pleased
a rag is a British student charity event, held to raise funds

explanation.surface: Pleased to go to charity events dressed in one's finest.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities, rag week is a series of student stunts to raise money for charity. The question mark flags that the rags are not literal rags.
explanation.definitionFit: Glad rags is an informal idiom for one's smartest party clothes.
